summary: A low-elevation Cascades lookout near Index, WA, rebuilt in 1964 with an experimental helicopter-delivered cab; now a Forest Service rental.

facts.design: Experimental 1963 Forest Products Laboratory cab (visually similar to, but not, an R-6 flattop); current structure built 1964

access.note: Open to hikers; cab rented overnight via recreation.gov.

visit.trail_note: About 3 miles round trip, moderate difficulty, some rocky footing

facts.agency: USDA Forest Service (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest)

events.note: 45-foot log tower with L-4 cab and ground-level sleeping room
Current timber tower (~63-67 ft) with experimental Forest Products Laboratory cab
Volunteers rebuilt the cab in the late 1990s, putting it back in usable shape

evidence.quote: Certainly one of the lowest elevation stations in the Washington Cascades
Heybrook was developed in 1925 with a platform tower, replaced by a 45' tower with L-4 cab in 1932

evidence.supports: 1925 tent platform; 1932 45-ft tower with ground room; rodents drove rangers up
evidence.quote: The first Heybrook fire lookout was a simple tent platform built in 1925. The Forest Service replaced it seven years later with a 45-foot log leg tower, with a ground-level cabin intended as sleeping quarters for fire rangers; however, rampant rodents eventually drove the rangers up into the tower where they lived until a 67-foot lookout was built in 1964.

evidence.supports: 1964 current 67-ft tower with R-6-style flat cab
evidence.quote: In 1964, the present 67' treated timber tower was built with an R-6 flat cab.

evidence.supports: current tower ~63 ft, cab looks like R-6 but is not
evidence.quote: This wooden tower, approximately 63 feet high, is standard but its cab is unique. It looks like an R-6 flattop design, but it is not.

evidence.supports: cab designed 1963 by Forest Products Lab for Region 6
evidence.quote: The cab was designed by the Forest Products Lab in 1963 at the request of the USFS Region 6 engineers.

evidence.supports: lightweight, helicopter-delivered, bundled like L-4 mule-train cabs; design not repeated
evidence.quote: Besides being lighter weight, the cab was to be prefabricated off site, then packed in bundles that could be delivered on site by helicopter. This a procedure similar to how the L-4 cabs of the 1930s were packaged to be delivered by mule train.
For whatever reason, cost or maintenance, this design has not been used again.
Promptly abandoned in 1970, volunteers worked on constructing a new cab during the late 1990's.
There is a group taking care of the lookout.

evidence.supports: views of Mount Index, Mount Persis, Wild Sky Wilderness
evidence.quote: On a clear day, guests at Heybrook Lookout see views of Mount Index and Bridal Veil Falls, Mount Baring, Mount Persis and the Wild Sky Wilderness.

corrections.proposed: Experimental 1963 Forest Products Laboratory cab (not a true R-6)
corrections.why: NHLR's register page states explicitly: 'It looks like an R-6 flattop design, but it is not,' and explains it was a one-off 1963 Forest Products Laboratory design for lightweight, helicopter-delivered construction.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1925 is the first lookout on the site (a tent platform, replaced in 1932 by a 45-ft tower); 1964 is the year the current timber tower and its experimental cab were built.

notes_for_editor: Height is unresolved: the tower record gives height_m 13.7 (~45 ft), but both NHLR (~63 ft) and firelookout.com (67 ft) describe the current 1964 tower as much taller; 13.7 m may describe the earlier 1932 tower instead. Worth a human check against the record's height_m field, but I did not propose a correction since I could not confirm which figure the record intends to describe. The location conflict between nhlr and ridb coordinates (787 m apart) was not resolved by available sources within budget.
